strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text decoding: repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate estimates of generalization.

The intended separation of both subjects and stimuli provides a sensible protocol for evaluating joint generalization to unseen people and language. The graph illustrations make these dependencies understandable.

Experiments cover two established models and both EEG and fMRI datasets. Additional held-out evaluation, shuffled-input controls, and the non-teacher-forced results in Table 6 provide useful evidence that evaluation choices substantially affect reported performance.
weaknesses: The supplied algorithms do not implement the central disjointness guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, excludes held-out subjects but permits adding their stimuli to training; Algorithm 2, line 33, excludes held-out stories but permits adding held-out subjects. These expansion rules contradict the requirement to check both endpoints in Equations 13–14. The implementation and resulting partitions need verification before the zero-leakage benchmark is reproducible.

Tables 3–5, including the proposed fair benchmark and shuffled-input analysis, use teacher forcing during generation, as Table 6 confirms. Access to gold target prefixes confounds conclusions about decoding from brain signals and memorization. For UniCoRN on ZuCo under split (c), BLEU-3 falls from 36.80 to 2.93 without teacher forcing. Table 6 is a useful partial control, but the additional-test-set and shuffled-input experiments also need evaluation under free generation.

The leakage metrics and reported decoding metrics require correction. Equation 17 uses signal-instance intersection to quantify subject overlap; disjoint EEG samples can share subjects without sharing signal instances. Its denominator is also zero for completely held-out subjects. Table 5 reports EEG2Text ROUGE-1 F1 of 25.74 with precision 23.95 and recall 23.98, which is inconsistent with standard F1 aggregation. Additionally, 40.65 is labeled ROUGE-1 F in Table 3 but R in Table 7. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the quantitative benchmark.

The claimed damage to encoder representations is not established by the evidence. Decreasing validation loss under overlapping subjects does not itself demonstrate overfitting or deteriorating representations; increasing test performance with longer training is likewise not proof of leakage. Evaluation on a common independent set is needed to substantiate these mechanisms. Comparisons between splitting strategies also change training-data quantity and evaluation difficulty, preventing attribution of the entire performance gap to leakage.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for a paper whose primary contribution is a splitting protocol. The manuscript provides some hyperparameters, but no code or split-manifest link, retained/discarded sample counts, precise construction and sizes of the additional test set, or clear specification of what is shuffled. Four-seed variability is reported only for leakage rates, without uncertainty for decoding results across subjects or partitions.

The assertion that all previous splitting methods are wrong exceeds the demonstrated scope. Subject-only and story-only splits evaluate different generalization targets and can be appropriate when those targets are explicitly stated. The paper should distinguish its joint unseen-subject/unseen-stimulus objective from those settings and assess prior work against its actual claims. Corrected algorithms, audited metrics, and controlled free-generation evaluation are substantive revisions needed before a sound Findings recommendation.
